     6	Is it true that, for all $k\neq 1$, there are infinitely many $n$ such that $2^n\equiv k\pmod{n}$?
     7	A conjecture of Graham. It is easy to see that $2^n\not\equiv 1\mod{n}$ for all $n>1$, so the restriction $k\neq 1$ is necessary. Erd\H{o}s and Graham report that Graham, Lehmer, and Lehmer have proved this for $k=2^i$ for $i\geq 1$, or if $k=-1$, but I cannot find such a paper. Tang has written a short
     8	note
     9	giving a proof for this case.
    10	As an indication of the difficulty, when $k=3$ the smallest $n$ such that $2^n\equiv 3\pmod{n}$ is $n=4700063497$.
    11	The minimal such $n$ for each $k$ is
    12	A036236
    13	in the OEIS.

3-Use this guide when you add or review a formalisation. The main question is whether the Lean

6:## Read the source and definitions
7-
8:Read the cited source, including relevant remarks and variants. Do not treat the module docstring
9:as an independent source. It is part of the change under review.

11-Read every non-standard definition used by the statement. Search Mathlib,
12-`FormalConjecturesForMathlib/`, and nearby files. Confirm names with `#check` and inspect their
13-definitions before you decide what they return on empty or smallest inputs.

23:- the order and scope of all quantifiers
24-- strict and non-strict bounds
25-- all hypotheses and domain restrictions
26-- equality, asymptotic equivalence, and order relations
27-- the direction of implications

31-Be careful with `∃ x, P x → Q`. The intended statement is usually `∃ x, P x ∧ Q`; the first
32-form can be trivially true.

34:For a yes-or-no problem, check that `answer(True)` states a positive answer and `answer(False)`
35:states a negative answer. Also check the scope and expected type of `answer(sorry)`. The rest of
36:the statement must constrain the unknown answer. It must not make the theorem true for every
37:possible answer.
